edits.before: Problem 2 (Major: Theorem 22 lacks a middle-extension or purity condition).  Appendix A, p. 23, assumes only that \(\mathcal F\) is elementary in the stated sense and has finite monodromy on a nonempty open set. It concludes that, on some nonempty open \(U_2\), its naive Fourier transform is a direct factor of \(R^1\pi_*\overline\mathbb Q_\ell\) for an abelian scheme. The conclusion is false even when the generic rank of \(\mathcal F\) is one.

Take \(k=\mathbb F_3\), \(\ell=2\), a nontrivial additive character \(\psi\) with values in \(\overline\mathbb Q_2^\times\), and \[j:\mathbb G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1,\qquad i:\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1,
 \qquad L=\mathcal L_{\psi(t^2)},\qquad \mathcal F=j_!j^*L.\] The generic monodromy has finite order three and is trivialized by an Artin–Schreier cover. The sheaf has no nonzero punctual sections, so it satisfies (Elem-1).

Take \(k=\mathbb F_3\), \(\ell=2\), a nontrivial additive character \(\psi\) with values in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_2^\times\), and \[j:\mathbb G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1,\qquad i:\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1,
 \qquad L=\mathcal L_{\psi(t^2)},\qquad \mathcal F=j_!j^*L.\] The generic monodromy has finite order three and is trivialized by an Artin–Schreier cover. The sheaf has no nonzero punctual sections, so it satisfies (Elem-1).

edits.before:
There is a short exact sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mathcal F\longrightarrow L
       \longrightarrow i_*\overline\mathbb Q_2\longrightarrow0.\] Tensor on \(\mathbb A^1_t\times\mathbb A^1_x\) with the Fourier kernel \(\mathcal L_{\psi(tx)}\) and apply \(Rp_{2!}\). The degree-zero compactly supported cohomology of the smooth rank-one sheaf \(\mathcal L_{\psi(t^2+xt)}\) is zero. The transform in degree zero of the punctual quotient is the constant sheaf. The long exact sequence therefore gives \[0\longrightarrow\overline\mathbb Q_2
    \longrightarrow \mathcal F_\psi(\mathcal F)
    \longrightarrow \mathcal F_\psi(L)\longrightarrow0.\] In particular, the Fourier transform contains a nonzero constant sub-local system on every nonempty open where it is lisse. At every closed point this contributes Frobenius eigenvalue \(1\).

edits.before: For an abelian scheme \(\pi:A\to U_2\), the eigenvalues of geometric Frobenius on \((R^1\pi_*\overline\mathbb Q_2)_s\) have complex absolute value \(|k(s)|^{1/2}>1\). It cannot contain that constant subrepresentation, and hence cannot contain the proposed Fourier transform even as a subobject, much less as a direct factor. Shrinking \(U_2\) cannot remove a constant sub-local system.

edits.before: Katz’s cited Theorem 7.3.8(5) was checked in the corrected author manuscript [katz], PDF pp. 211–213 (Chapter 7 local pp. 11–13). Its use of purity is governed by Definition 7.3.7, which requires a middle extension in addition to purity on a lisse open. Definition 7.3.5 likewise distinguishes Fourier sheaves from merely elementary ones. Here \(\mathcal F\) is not a middle extension: its stalk at zero is zero, while \(L_0=\overline\mathbb Q_2\). Thus the cited theorem does not supply the purity asserted in the paper.

Let \(k=\mathbb F_3\), \(S=\mathbb A^1/k\), \(\ell=2\), and let \[\rho:\pi_1(S)\longrightarrow\widehat\mathbb Z\longrightarrow\mathbb Z_2
   \longrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_2),\qquad
 n\longmapsto u(n)=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\] where the arithmetic projection sends geometric Frobenius to \(1\). Its compact image is isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z_2\), and conjugacy in that image is trivial.
